operations.before: Since every element of $G$ is its own inverse, $S(p_x\#u_g)=p_x\#u_g$. In $m(S\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta(p_x\#u_g)$, a summand survives exactly when $a=b$ in $ab=x$; this is impossible when $x=s$, and for $x=e$ the two surviving terms sum to $p_e\#u_e+p_s\#u_e=1_D$. The same calculation gives $m(\operatorname{id}\otimes S)\Delta(p_x\#u_g)$. These values equal $\varepsilon(p_x\#u_g)1_D$, so both antipode identities hold and $D(k^G)$ is a Hopf algebra.

operations.before: For $d=p_y\#u_g$, expanding the two sides with the displayed product gives $R\Delta(d)=\sum_{ab=y}(p_a\#u_g)\otimes(p_b\#u_{ag})$ and $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(d)R=\sum_{ab=y}(p_b\#u_g)\otimes(p_a\#u_{gb})$. Since $G$ is abelian, $u_{gb}=u_{bg}$; interchanging $a$ and $b$ preserves the condition $ab=y$ and makes the latter sum equal to the former. Bilinearity extends equality from the basis to all $d\in D(k^G)$.
